sections.h2: What the Utah homestead exemption means
sections.html:
In Utah the word covers two separate protections: a creditor protection for equity in your home, and a property tax reduction for primary residences. They sit in different parts of the Utah Code and are handled by different offices.

The creditor protection is in the Utah Exemptions Act, Utah Code 78B-5-503 and 78B-5-504, and it is enforced in court. The tax reduction is in Utah Code 59-2-103 and 59-2-103.5, and your county assessor applies it. A homeowner preparing to sell may care about both, and mixing them up leads to wrong assumptions about who to call.

sections.h2: How much of a Utah home is protected from creditors
sections.html:
A primary personal residence is exempt up to $42,000 in value, and other property up to $5,000. Those figures are adjusted for inflation each year, so check the current numbers with the state.

Utah homestead exemption amounts
Protected propertyAmount
Primary personal residence, one owner$42,000
Other property, one owner$5,000
Jointly owned primary residence, household maximum$84,000
Other property, household maximum$10,000
Land counted with the homeUp to one acre reasonably necessary for its use

A primary personal residence is a dwelling or mobile home where you and your household live, plus the surrounding land up to one acre. A household here means people related by blood or marriage who live together as an economic unit.

sections.h2: Debts the homestead does not protect against
sections.html:
The homestead is not a shield against every claim. Section 78B-5-503 lists the exceptions, and a lender or the county can still reach the house in these cases.

  • Statutory liens for property taxes and assessments.
  • Security interests and judicial liens for the purchase price.
  • Judicial liens for unpaid child support or maintenance.
  • Consensual liens created by a contract, such as a mortgage or trust deed.
  • Calls or assessments on water rights used for the homestead.
  • Property acquired through criminal activity.

In practice the exemption matters most to an owner with unsecured debt, such as a judgment or a credit card balance, who wants to know whether the house can be forced to a sale.

Under Utah Code 78B-5-504 you claim it by filing a signed and acknowledged declaration with the recorder of the county where the property sits. You can also serve it on the sheriff or officer running an execution before the time stated in the notice of execution.

The declaration must include the following items:

  • A claim of exemption and, if married, a statement that your spouse has not filed one.
  • A description of the property and an estimated cash value.
  • The amount of homestead you are claiming.
  • The name, age and address of any spouse and dependents.

If you do not file or serve it as required, title passes to the purchaser at the execution sale free of homestead rights. For married owners, a conveyance, security interest or contract to convey homestead property is valid only if both spouses sign, which also matters when you sell.

sections.h2: Can a Utah homestead be sold at an execution sale?
sections.html:
Homestead property cannot be sold at execution unless a bid exceeds the declared exemption amount. A sale is subject to the debtor's right of redemption under Rule 69C of the Utah Rules of Civil Procedure, and if there is a deficiency the property cannot be taken again to cover it.

An owner facing an execution sale should get advice from a Utah attorney about how the proceeds are divided.

sections.h2: Money from selling a Utah homestead
sections.html:
Sale proceeds up to the exemption amount at the time of sale are exempt from levy, execution or other process for one year after you receive them. A sale also does not stop you from claiming or buying another homestead.

That one year window is useful when you sell and plan to buy elsewhere. Keep the closing statement and deposit records together so you can show where the exempt money came from.

sections.h2: The primary residential exemption for property tax
sections.html:
Utah allows a 45% reduction in the fair market value of residential property for a calendar year, so a qualifying home is taxed on 55% of its value. The exemption applies to one primary residence per household and to no more than one acre of land per residential unit.

The home must be a primary domicile occupied for at least 183 consecutive days in a calendar year, by the owner or by a full-time tenant. Vacation and second homes do not qualify. A home that becomes residential after January 1 can qualify as part-year property if it is used as a residence for 183 or more consecutive days that year.

  • 90 days: time to return the primary residence declaration after the county's notice.
  • 30 days: time to file after a second notice, or lose the exemption for that year.
  • September 15: application deadline, and late applications cannot be accepted.
  • 183 days: consecutive days of occupancy needed.
  • November 30: property tax due date.

Missing the deadline can mean being taxed on 100% of market value for that year.

The exemption does not carry over to new owners, who must file their own application. Starting January 1, 2027, an ownership change, including a deed, a trust transfer or a name update, requires a TC-473A filing with the county board of equalization.

Under Utah Code 59-2-103.5, an owner who no longer qualifies must tell the county on a form and declare the change on the Utah income tax return. That notice is not required when the owner moves to a new primary residence and qualifies for it.

  • Check your valuation notice, mailed each year on or before July 22, to see whether the exemption is applied.
  • Tell the county if the home stops being your primary residence.
  • Expect the buyer to file a new application.
  • Pay or prorate the November 30 tax at closing.

sections.h2: If the house is rented out
sections.html:
A rental can still qualify if it is a tenant's primary residence. Utah Code 59-2-103 allows the exemption for each residential property that is a tenant's primary residence, and the owner files a declaration under penalty of perjury.

The assessor may ask for a signed lease. If that falls short, the assessor may ask for an insurance policy and then a federal tax return showing rental profit or loss. The county may not contact the tenant directly. The owner's own home has to be a separate primary residence for the one per household rule.

Utah has several relief programs beyond the 45% exemption, and counties make the first call on eligibility. Each has its own form number.

  • Homeowner's tax credit: form TC-90H.
  • Renter refund: form TC-90CB.
  • Low-income abatement: form TC-90L.
  • Delinquent tax deferral or settlement: form PT-33, with PT-33A for a lienholder agreement.
  • Active-duty armed forces exemption (PT-22), veteran with a disability exemption (PT-25) and blind persons exemption (PT-31).

The valuation notice must also tell owners who are 65 or older, disabled or facing extreme hardship that they may be able to defer tax on a primary residence. Deferred amounts are a lien, which matters at closing.

sections.h2: Selling a Utah house for cash
sections.html:
If the house has tax due, judgment liens or a mortgage behind, the homestead does not stop a sale and does not erase those claims. It protects equity from certain creditors, and the proceeds stay protected for a year.

Cash Home Buyers buys Utah houses as-is, including houses with inherited title, tenants or delinquent tax. If you are weighing a sale, tell us what liens or notices are recorded and we can look at the numbers with your title company.

faqs.q: How much is the Utah homestead exemption?
faqs.a: $42,000 for a primary personal residence and $5,000 for other property, with a household maximum of $84,000 for a jointly owned primary residence. The figures are adjusted for inflation each year, so confirm the current amounts.

faqs.q: Do I have to file a homestead declaration in Utah?
faqs.a: Yes, to claim it. Utah Code 78B-5-504 calls for a signed, acknowledged declaration with the county recorder, or service on the officer running an execution before the time in the notice of execution. Without it, title can pass to the buyer at an execution sale free of homestead rights.

faqs.q: What is the Utah primary residential exemption deadline?
faqs.a: September 15 for applications. Late applications cannot be accepted, and missing the date can mean being taxed on 100% of market value for that year.

faqs.q: Is the Utah homestead exemption transferable to a buyer?
faqs.a: No. The property tax exemption does not carry over to new owners. A buyer files a new application, and from January 1, 2027, an ownership change requires form TC-473A with the county board of equalization.

faqs.q: Are my sale proceeds protected after I sell my Utah home?
faqs.a: Partly. Proceeds up to the exemption amount at the time of sale are exempt from levy or execution for one year after you receive them, and you may claim or buy another homestead.
